title: The questions
hookLine: three questions in the grave: who is your Lord, what is your religion, who is this man

lines: NO NOTES, NO LOOKING IT UP.
cards: Who is your Lord? What is your religion? Who is this man who was sent among you?
Three questions. No multiple choice, no notes, no time to look anything up. In the hadith that tell of the grave, two angels ask them, soon after the mourners have walked away.
One hadith in Sahih al-Bukhari even says the dead person hears the footsteps of the people leaving. Then the questions begin.

teach.h: TWO ANGELS SIT THE PERSON UP.
teach.b: The long hadith of al-Bara' ibn 'Azib, collected by Abu Dawud, lays it out. Two angels come and sit the person up. Who is your Lord?
The believer says: my Lord is Allah. What is your religion? My religion is Islam.
Who is this man who was sent among you? He is the Messenger of Allah. A hadith in Tirmidhi gives the two angels names: Munkar and Nakir.
Then the other side of the scene. The one who lived without faith is asked the same three questions, and the answer, in paraphrase, is: I don't know.
I heard people saying something, so I said it. That's the whole failure. Not a wrong theory.
A borrowed answer, repeated without ever being one's own.

teach.h: A FIRM SAYING, HELD IN LIFE.
teach.b: The Qur'an has a verse that a hadith in Bukhari ties to this moment, in Pickthall's words: "Allah confirmeth those who believe by a firm saying in the life of the world and in the Hereafter."

The answer holds in the grave because it was held in life. Some teachers draw a plain lesson from it. You can't memorize your way through these questions the night before, because they aren't testing memory.
They ask what you actually lived by. Who did you turn to when it counted? What way did you follow on an ordinary day?
Whose example did you keep? That's today's line: answer now. The exam is set in advance, and every day is a chance to work on the answers.

how: Muslims teach the three questions of the grave to children, and at burials those present may pray for the deceased to be made firm when the angels question them.

games.q: in the hadith, two angels ask the one who lived without faith: who is this man sent among you? what does he answer?
o: he is the Messenger of Allah.
I don't know. I heard people saying something, so I said it.
games.why: a borrowed answer: something repeated, never made one's own. the hadith's failure is not a wrong theory but an answer never lived.

practice: Take the three questions slowly, in your own words: who or what did I actually turn to this week when things went wrong; what way do I live by when no one is watching; whose example am I following?
If you're Muslim, you may want to say the answers the hadith gives, and ask whether this week said them too; if you're not, let your honest answers be what they are, without judging them.
